summary: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a BST.
mainInsight: In a BST the LCA is the first node whose value lies between p and q (inclusive): if both are larger go right, if both are smaller go left, otherwise this node is the split point.
canonicalApproach: Walk down using the BST order

approaches.name: Generic tree LCA
approaches.summary: Postorder search for p and q in both subtrees.

approaches.name: Walk down using the BST order
approaches.summary: Move left or right until p and q are separated.

personalSolution.approach: Walk down using the BST order (recursive)
personalSolution.notes: Optimal; an iterative loop gives O(1) space.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Walk down from the root using the BST order until p and q fall on different sides. Clue: It is a BST, so comparing p and q with the current value says which side holds both; the first node where they separate is the lowest common ancestor.
keyPoints: It is a BST, so comparing p and q with the current value says which side holds both; the first node where they separate is the lowest common ancestor.
cards.explanation: The BST order tells you where each target lies, so the first node between p and q is the answer and one root-to-node walk suffices.

rubric.technique: Walk down from the root using the BST order until p and q fall on different sides
aliases: compare values with p and q

rubric.clue: It is a BST, so comparing p and q with the current value says which side holds both; the first node where they separate is the lowest common ancestor.

promptVariants: How does the BST property simplify the LCA?
When is the current node the LCA?
options: When p and q lie on different sides (or one equals the node)
When both p and q lie in the left subtree of the node
When the node is the root of the whole tree and nothing else
When the node has two children below it in the tree
cards.answer: When p and q lie on different sides (or one equals the node)
cards.explanation: If they diverge here, no deeper node can be an ancestor of both.

incorrectOptionExplanations.When both p and q lie in the left subtre: Then the LCA is deeper, in the left subtree.
incorrectOptionExplanations.When the node is the root of the whole t: Only if they diverge at the root.

promptVariants: Why can you ignore one subtree at every step?
What does `root.val < p.val and root.val < q.val` mean?
cards.answer: If both p and q are greater than the current node, both lie in the right subtree (BST order), so the LCA is in the right subtree; symmetrically for smaller. Once they are not on the same side, the current node separates them and is the lowest common ancestor.
keyPoints: Otherwise the split point is the LCA
cards.explanation: A node may be its own ancestor.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Time complexity (h = height): ___
How can you make it O(1)?
cards.answer: Recursion uses O(h) stack; an iterative loop that moves the `root` pointer uses O(1) extra space.
cards.explanation: Easy to convert since it is tail recursion.

promptVariants: What is the LCA when one node is an ancestor of the other?
How does the code return it?
options: The ancestor itself: it is not strictly left or right of both
The parent of the ancestor node, one level above that node
None, because the nodes are not on different sides of it
The root, whatever the positions of p and q in the tree
cards.answer: The ancestor itself: it is not strictly left or right of both
cards.explanation: A node can be a descendant of itself, so the LCA of a node and its descendant is the node.
